For one-way server-to-browser updates, use **Server-Sent Events (SSE)**. If you also need the browser to send messages back, use **WebSockets**.

**Server-Sent Events (recommended for one-way push)**
- It uses the `text/event-stream` format, which is supported natively by browsers with the `EventSource` API.[1]
- SSE is commonly used for AI chat streaming, live notifications, logs and observability, and other cases where the server pushes updates to the client.[1]
- Each event is a small text block with "fields" like `data`, `event`, `id`, and `retry`, separated by blank lines.[1]
- It was added in FastAPI 0.135.0.[1]

The excerpt I have doesn't include the code for an SSE endpoint. See the rest of the [Server-Sent Events tutorial](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/server-sent-events/) for the implementation.

**WebSockets (two-way communication)**
First, add `websockets` (a Python library that makes it easy to use the "WebSocket" protocol) to your project[2]. Then define a WebSocket route:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket

app = FastAPI()

@app.websocket("/ws")
async def websocket_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket):
    await websocket.accept()
    while True:
        data = await websocket.receive_text()
        await websocket.send_text(f"Message text was: {data}")
```

In the browser, you'd connect with `new WebSocket("ws://localhost:8000/ws")` and handle messages in `ws.onmessage`. You can receive and send binary, text, and JSON data.[4]

If you're broadcasting to many clients, note that keeping connections in memory will only work while the process is running, and will only work with a single process.[3] For something more robust, check encode/broadcaster[3].
